title: How do hidden classes compare to dynamically generated `Proxy` classes, and how do they behave under JPMS module restrictions?
shortTitle: Hidden classes vs dynamically generated `Proxy` classes, and their behaviour under JPMS module restrictions

s1_definition.profdef: Dynamically generated `Proxy` classes, created by `java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance`, are normal, named, loader-registered classes that implement a list of interfaces and route calls through an `InvocationHandler`. Hidden classes, created by `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass`, are nameless, loader-unregistered, independently unloadable classes usable only through a direct reference. Under the Java Platform Module System, a `Proxy` for non-public interfaces is placed in a dynamic module and requires the interfaces to be accessible, whereas a hidden class is defined in the same runtime package and module as its lookup class, inheriting that module's access and readability.
s1_definition.analogy: A `Proxy` is like National Bank of India creating a new, officially-named stand-in counter that is listed in the branch directory and follows the bank's visitor rules about which departments it may enter. A hidden class is like a private, unnamed helper created inside a specific manager's office — it is not in the directory, only that manager can use it, and it automatically has the same office keys and department membership as the manager who made it. One is a public, directory-listed stand-in; the other is a private, same-room helper that inherits its creator's access.
s1_definition.oneliner: A `Proxy` is a named, registered, interface-based class in a dynamic module; a hidden class is nameless, unregistered, unloadable, and lives in its lookup class's own module and package.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Dynamically generated `Proxy` classes, created by `java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance`, are normal, named, loader-registered classes that implement a list of interfaces and route calls through an `InvocationHandler`. Hidden classes, created by `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass`, are nameless, loader-unregistered, independently unloadable classes usable only through a direct reference. Under the Java Platform Module System, a `Proxy` for non-public interfaces is placed in a dynamic module and requires the interfaces to be accessible, whereas a hidden class is defined in the same runtime package and module as its lookup class, inheriting that module's access and readability.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A `Proxy` is like National Bank of India creating a new, officially-named stand-in counter that is listed in the branch directory and follows the bank's visitor rules about which departments it may enter. A hidden class is like a private, unnamed helper created inside a specific manager's office — it is not in the directory, only that manager can use it, and it automatically has the same office keys and department membership as the manager who made it. One is a public, directory-listed stand-in; the other is a private, same-room helper that inherits its creator's access.

**One line to remember:** A `Proxy` is a named, registered, interface-based class in a dynamic module; a hidden class is nameless, unregistered, unloadable, and lives in its lookup class's own module and package.

sections.s2_technical:
A **dynamic `Proxy`** is created with `Proxy.newProxyInstance(classLoader, interfaces, handler)`. The JVM generates a class that implements all the listed interfaces, and every method call is dispatched to the `handler.invoke(proxy, method, args)` method, where you add behaviour and delegate. The generated proxy class is a **normal class**: it has a real binary name such as `com.sun.proxy.$Proxy0` or a name in a dynamic module, it is registered in the class loader, and it lives as long as the loader. Proxies are limited to **interfaces** — they cannot proxy concrete classes, which is why Spring falls back to CGLIB subclassing when there is no interface.

A **hidden class** is created from raw bytecode via `defineHiddenClass`. It is **not registered** in the loader, has no usable binary name, cannot be referenced by other classes' constant pools, and can be **unloaded independently** when unreachable. It can implement any interface or even extend a class, because you supply arbitrary bytecode, not just an interface list. It can be a nestmate of its host for private access. So hidden classes are far more flexible than proxies but require you to generate bytecode yourself, whereas `Proxy` generates the bytecode for you from a simple interface list.

The practical **comparison**: use `Proxy` when you just need an interface-based wrapper with a single dispatch point and do not want to generate bytecode by hand — it is simple and built in. Use a hidden class when you are a framework that generates specialised classes, needs them invisible and unloadable, needs private access to a host, or needs to implement something richer than a pure interface dispatch. Modern JDK machinery such as the lambda metafactory uses hidden classes; application code wiring simple interface interceptors often still uses `Proxy` or a library like ByteBuddy.

Under **JPMS (the module system)**, `Proxy` behaviour depends on interface accessibility. If all the proxied interfaces are **public and in exported packages**, the proxy is defined in a **dynamic module** that reads the necessary modules, and it works. If any interface is **non-public**, all such interfaces must be in the **same package** and the same module, and the proxy is defined in that package, so the package's module must allow it. Proxies cannot bridge interfaces that live in packages the proxy's module cannot read or access, and this trips people up when interfaces are not exported or opened.

A **hidden class under JPMS** behaves more simply because it is defined in the **same runtime package and the same module** as the lookup class used to create it. It therefore inherits exactly that module's readability and access: it can read whatever the lookup class's module reads, and with `NESTMATE` it can access the lookup class's private members directly. There is no separate dynamic module, and no requirement to export or open additional packages for the hidden class itself, because it is effectively part of the lookup class's module. This makes hidden classes a cleaner fit for strongly-encapsulated modular applications, which is one more reason the JDK adopted them internally.

A senior nuance is that because a hidden class shares the lookup class's protection domain and module, it is subject to the **same module boundaries** — it cannot magically access a package that its host module cannot access, so it does not weaken encapsulation. Another nuance is that a `Proxy` over interfaces from **multiple modules** must have all those interfaces accessible, and the generated proxy module is given appropriate `reads` edges automatically, but non-exported interfaces still require being in one package. A final nuance is that for frameworks migrating off `Unsafe` or needing fine lifecycle control in modular apps, hidden classes avoid the dynamic-module complexity that proxies introduce.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to wrap its `AccountService` interface with a logging interceptor without writing a hand-coded wrapper. The simplest built-in tool is a dynamic `Proxy` that implements the interface and routes every call through a handler that logs and delegates. This shows the `Proxy` approach and its interface-only limitation.

Problem 2 — The bank's framework team instead generates a specialised, invisible, unloadable implementation class per deployment that needs private access to a host engine. A `Proxy` cannot give private host access or independent unloading, so they use a hidden class via `defineHiddenClass` with `NESTMATE`. This contrasts the two mechanisms directly.

Problem 3 — The services run in a modular (JPMS) application. We show that the `Proxy` works because the interface is public and exported, and that the hidden class simply inherits the lookup class's module and package, needing no extra exports. This makes the module behaviour concrete.

In the mini-project we define an `AccountService` interface and real implementation, create a logging `Proxy` around it, define a hidden class that reads a host private value via `NESTMATE`, and log how each behaves and how modules affect them.

The code contains: an `AccountService`, a `RealAccountService`, a `LoggingHandler` for the proxy, a `HiddenFactory` host, and a `main`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile (Java 15+ for defineHiddenClass)
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/pvh/ProxyVsHiddenDemo.java

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.pvh.ProxyVsHiddenDemo

# As a module (JPMS): proxy uses a dynamic module; hidden class stays in com.bank.pvh
java --module-path target/classes -m com.bank.pvh/com.bank.pvh.ProxyVsHiddenDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request for Rajesh's balance (SAV2001, 1,000,000) through a proxy, and a fee of 0.1% on 1,000,000 through a hidden class.

Step 1 — `main` creates the real `AccountService` and wraps it with `Proxy.newProxyInstance`, passing the class loader, the single interface, and a `LoggingHandler`. The JVM generates a named, registered proxy class implementing `AccountService`.

Step 2 — We log the proxy's class name, which is a real binary name in a JDK proxy module, showing it is a normal, discoverable class. Calling `getBalance("SAV2001")` routes through the handler, which logs before, delegates to the real object returning 1,000,000, logs after, and returns.

Step 3 — `main` creates a `HiddenFactory` whose `rate` field is private. It calls `feeViaHidden(1000000)`.

Step 4 — The factory reads the bytecode of `HiddenCalc`, obtains a lookup, and calls `defineHiddenClass` with `NESTMATE`. The hidden class is created in the factory's own module and package, so it needs no extra module exports. Being a nestmate, it reads the host's private rate through the accessor.

Step 5 — The hidden calculator computes 0.1% of 1,000,000, which is 1,000.00, using `BigDecimal` with half-up rounding, and returns it. The hidden class is eligible for unloading once unreachable, unlike the proxy which lives with its loader.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Proxy class name = jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] PROXY before getBalance args=[SAV2001]
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] PROXY after  getBalance result=1000000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Proxy balance SAV2001 = Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Hidden class fee (NESTMATE read host private rate) = Rs.1000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  PROXY path (interface-based, named, registered)
    Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, [AccountService], LoggingHandler)
      │ generates jdk.proxyN/$ProxyM  (normal class, in dynamic module)
      ▼
    proxy.getBalance("SAV2001")
      │ → handler.invoke(proxy, getBalance, [SAV2001])
      │     log before → real.getBalance → 1,000,000 → log after
      ▼
    returns 1,000,000

  HIDDEN path (bytecode, nameless, unloadable, same module)
    HiddenFactory(rate=0.001 PRIVATE)
      │ lookup.defineHiddenClass(HiddenCalc bytes, true, NESTMATE)
      │   → hidden class in com.bank.pvh (lookup's module) — no extra exports
      ▼
    new HiddenCalc(factory) → NESTMATE reads host private rate
      │ 1,000,000 × 0.001 = 1000.00
      ▼
    returns 1000.00  (eligible to unload when unreachable)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A dynamically generated Proxy class, created by Proxy dot newProxyInstance, is a normal, named, loader-registered class that implements a list of interfaces and routes every call through an invocation handler. Because it is interface-based, it cannot proxy a concrete class, which is why Spring falls back to CGLIB subclassing when there is no interface. A hidden class, created by defineHiddenClass, is nameless, not registered in the loader, cannot be referenced by name from other classes, and can be unloaded independently when it becomes unreachable. It is defined from arbitrary bytecode, so it can implement any interface or even extend a class, and with NESTMATE it can access its host's private members.

So the comparison I give is: use a Proxy when I just need a simple interface wrapper with one dispatch point and do not want to generate bytecode myself, because it is built in and easy. Use a hidden class when I am writing framework-level code that generates specialised classes and needs them invisible, unloadable, able to touch a host's private state, or richer than a pure interface dispatch. The JDK's own lambda metafactory uses hidden classes, while application-level interface interception often still uses Proxy. In my banking project I wrap the account service with a logging Proxy for simple interception, and I use a hidden class for a generated fee calculator that reads a private rate on its host.

Under the module system the two behave differently. A Proxy's behaviour depends on interface accessibility: if the interfaces are public and exported, the proxy goes into a dynamic module that is given the right reads edges and it just works, but if any interface is non-public, all such interfaces must sit in the same package and module. A hidden class is simpler because it is defined in the same runtime package and module as the lookup class that created it, so it inherits that module's readability and access and needs no extra exports, and with NESTMATE it reads the host's privates directly.

The important nuance I add is that a hidden class does not weaken encapsulation, because it shares the host module's protection domain and therefore cannot reach a package the host module itself cannot reach. That clean module fit, plus independent unloading and private host access, is exactly why the JDK adopted hidden classes internally and why I reach for them in framework code, while keeping Proxy for straightforward interface interception in ordinary application code.
